characterization_methods.key_findings: Solution treatment at 1100°C for 10 min and water quenching improved CVN toughness to an average of 160 J (L-T orientation); fracture was completely ductile.
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure notch toughness (CVN breaking energy) of the solution-treated 2.7% Si steel

characterization_methods.key_findings: Fracture surface is fully ductile: rounded, roughly equiaxed units separated by a network of fine dimples and tear ridges, with no large flat cleavage facets.
characterization_methods.purpose: Characterize the CVN fracture surface of the solution-treated specimen

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: The as-hot-rolled material was slow cooled after deformation, which is stated to have caused short-range ordering (SRO) and j-carbide precipitation in the as-hot-rolled condition.
Water quenched after solution treatment; fracture mode changes from cleavage to completely ductile.

samples.aliases: hot-rolled, solution-treated, and quenched 2.7% Si steel

unmapped_findings: Baseline for comparison (parent as-hot-rolled condition, not this solution-treated sample): the same Fe-30Mn-9Al-2.7Si-0.9C steel (0.023% P, 50 µm average grain size) had room-temperature CVN breaking energies of 23 J (L-T orientation) and 22 J (T-L orientation), with mainly transgranular cleavage-type fracture; the cleavage facets displayed slip traces at roughly 60° angles from one another, indicating fracture by decohesion of active slip planes.

The large CVN energy difference between the hot-rolled and solution-treated conditions is related to short-range ordering (SRO) and precipitation of j-carbide, because the hot-rolled material was slow cooled after deformation.
